You are an AI assistant tasked with solving command-line tasks in a Linux environment. You will be given a task description and the output from previously executed commands. Your goal is to solve the task by providing batches of shell commands.

Format your response as JSON with the following structure:

{{
  "analysis": "Analyze the current state based on the terminal output provided. What do you see? What has been accomplished? What still needs to be done?",
  "plan": "Describe your plan for the next steps. What commands will you run and why? Be specific about what you expect each command to accomplish.",
  "commands": [
    {{
      "keystrokes": "ls -la\\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    }},
    {{
      "keystrokes": "cd project\\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    }}
  ],
  "task_complete": true
}}

Required fields:
- "analysis": Your analysis of the current situation
- "plan": Your plan for the next steps
- "commands": Array of command objects to execute

Optional fields:
- "task_complete": Boolean indicating if the task is complete (defaults to false if not present)

Command object structure:
- "keystrokes": String containing the exact keystrokes to send to the terminal (required)
- "duration": Number of seconds to wait for the command to complete (defaults to 1.0 if not present)

IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used as shell commands.
- Most bash commands should end with a newline (\n) to cause them to execute
- For special key sequences, use: C-c for Ctrl+C, C-d for Ctrl+D

The "duration" attribute specifies wait time:
- 0.1 seconds for instant commands (cd, ls, echo, cat)
- 1.0 seconds for normal commands (gcc, find, rustc)
- 5-30 seconds for slow commands (make, python scripts, wget)

Important notes:
- Each command's keystrokes are executed in sequence
- Do not include extra whitespace unless it's part of the command
- The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes
- Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action
- Set task_complete to true ONLY when the task is fully finished and verified
- CRITICAL: BEFORE writing any code or modifying files, you MUST explore the workspace and read the provided documentation (e.g., `cat skill.md` or `cat task_spec.json`) to learn the required skills and constraints.
- DO NOT rely solely on your pre-trained knowledge. Base your implementation strictly on the context provided in the workspace documents.

Task Description:
Convert the technical discussion into a full TED-style talk. Use the main insight from the conversation, keep it concrete, and include an opening hook plus a Q&A section. Save the final talk as output.txt in the workspace.

it matters, with examples concrete enough to apply and implications broad enough to inspire."

    {
      "keystrokes": "cat > output.txt << 'EOF'
================================================================================
                    THE SPEED ILLUSION
              Why Slowing Down Makes You Faster
                    A TED-Style Talk
================================================================================

[OPENING HOOK]

Imagine this: You're standing on a construction site. A team of engineers is
racing to build a bridge. They're working around the clock. Every hour counts.
They're cutting corners, skipping inspections, pushing harder and faster.

And the bridge collapses.

Not because they weren't fast enough.
But because they were moving too fast to learn.

Now imagine a different team. They move deliberately. They pause to ask:
"Are we building the right bridge?" "What assumptions are we making?"
"What could go wrong?"

They take time to capture their uncertainties. They validate their assumptions.
They codify their learnings into patterns that everyone can use.

And their bridge stands.

This isn't just about bridges. This is about software. About teams.
About the systems we build to innovate.

[THE PROBLEM]

A few years ago, I worked with a team that had built what should have been
the perfect experimentation platform. They could spin up environments in
minutes. Deploy code in seconds. Test hypotheses at breakneck speed.

On paper, it was revolutionary.

In practice? It was a disaster.

Teams were churning out experiments at an incredible rate. But they were
repeating the same mistakes. They were rediscovering the same problems.
They were optimizing for local speed—how fast could I ship my feature?
—instead of shared learning—what can we all learn from this?

The system wasn't failing because of code generation.
It wasn't failing because of infrastructure.

It was failing because of decision latency.

[THE CORE INSIGHT]

Decision latency. That's the time between making a decision and learning
whether that decision was right.

In traditional software development, decision latency can be months.
You build something. You ship it. You wait for metrics. You analyze.
You decide. You iterate.

The faster experimentation platforms promised to reduce this. And in one
sense, they did. You can ship faster.

But here's the paradox: When you ship faster without learning faster,
you don't reduce decision latency. You just accumulate more decisions
whose outcomes you haven't yet learned.

The real bottleneck isn't how fast you can write code.
The real bottleneck is how fast you can learn from what you've built.

[THE THREE-STAGE RHYTHM]

So what's the solution? How do we actually reduce decision latency?

We introduced a three-stage rhythm:

Stage 1: Capture Uncertainty

Before you write a single line of code, ask: What don't we know?
What are the risks? What assumptions are we making?

This sounds simple. But most teams skip it. They jump straight to
implementation because implementation feels like progress.

But capturing uncertainty is progress. It's the progress of clarity.

Stage 2: Validate Assumptions

Now you build. But you build to learn, not to ship.
You design small-scale pilots that test your riskiest assumptions.
You release reviews that surface what's working and what isn't.
You incident retrospectives that turn failures into lessons.

The goal isn't perfection. The goal is learning.

Stage 3: Codify the Pattern

This is where most teams fail. They learn something valuable. They fix
a problem. And they move on.

But if you don't codify what you've learned, the next team will rediscover
it. The next engineer will make the same mistake.

Codifying means: Document the pattern. Create the checklist. Build the
tool. Make the learning available to everyone.

[CONCRETE EXAMPLES]

Let me give you some concrete examples of what this looks like in practice.

Example 1: Release Reviews

Instead of shipping and hoping, one team instituted a mandatory release
review. Every deployment required answering three questions:

- What did we expect to happen?
- What actually happened?
- What will we do differently next time?

This took an extra 30 minutes per release. But it reduced production
incidents by 40% in six months. Why? Because the team was learning.

Example 2: Incident Retrospectives

When something broke, the team didn't just fix it and move on. They held
a retrospective. They asked: What assumptions did we make that turned
out to be wrong? How can we catch this earlier next time?

One retrospective led to a new monitoring dashboard. Another led to a
new deployment pattern. Each incident became an investment in future speed.

Example 3: Small-Scale Pilots

Instead of rolling out a feature to everyone, teams started with pilots.
They'd launch to 5% of users. They'd watch. They'd learn. They'd iterate.

This felt slower at first. But it prevented costly rollbacks. It prevented
disappointing full launches. It turned uncertainty into clarity.

[ADDRESSING THE CONCERNS]

Now, I know what you're thinking. "This sounds like bureaucracy."
"This sounds like it will slow us down."
"We can't afford to move slower."

These are legitimate concerns. And they're exactly what the team said
when we proposed this approach.

But here's what happened: Rework went down.

Not up. Down.

Because we were learning faster. Because we were making better decisions.
Because we weren't building things we didn't need, fixing bugs we could
have prevented, or rediscovering solutions that already existed.

The three-stage rhythm didn't slow them down. It eliminated the hidden
costs of not learning: rework, repetition, and preventable failures.

[THE BIGGER PICTURE]

This isn't just about software engineering. This is about any system
designed for innovation.

Research labs. Product teams. Startups. Even governments.

Anyplace where we're trying to learn our way forward will face the same
challenge: The temptation to optimize for local speed instead of shared
learning.

And the same solution: A rhythm that captures uncertainty, validates
assumptions, and codifies patterns.

[THE CALL TO ACTION]

So here's my challenge to you:

Look at your team. Look at your processes. Look at how you make decisions.

Are you optimizing for local speed? Or are you optimizing for shared
learning?

Are you capturing uncertainty? Or are you pretending you know everything?

Are you validating assumptions? Or are you assuming you're right?

Are you codifying patterns? Or are you letting knowledge die with each
person who leaves?

The fastest way forward isn't to move faster. It's to learn faster.

And the fastest way to learn is to slow down enough to actually see what
you're building.

[Q&A SECTION]

Q: How do you balance this approach with aggressive deadlines?

A: Great question. The key is to think of this as risk management.
When deadlines are tight, you have less time to learn. That means you
need to be even more intentional about capturing uncertainty and
validating assumptions. A 30-minute session to clarify what you don't
know can save days of building the wrong thing.

Q: How do you convince leadership to invest in this?

A: Show them the cost of not doing it. Track rework. Track repeat
incidents. Track time spent fixing preventable problems. Then show
them how much of that disappears when you invest in learning. The
ROI is real—it just takes a few cycles to measure.

Q: What if my team resists this approach?

A: Start small. Pick one process—maybe release reviews or incident
retrospectives—and do it well. Show the value. Then expand. People
resist change until they see it works. Your job is to make it work
for them first.

Q: How do you measure success?

A: Look at decision latency. How long from decision to learning?
Look at rework rates. How often are you redoing work? Look at
knowledge retention. When someone leaves, how much do you lose?
These are the metrics that matter.

Q: Is this scalable to large organizations?

A: Absolutely. In fact, it's more important at scale. The more people
you have, the more critical it is to capture and share learning.
The three-stage rhythm provides a common language and process that
works at any size.

================================================================================
                              THANK YOU
================================================================================
